report:
The dispute concerns a suit for specific performance and compensation brought by Kalyanpur Lime Works Ltd. (the Lime Co.) against the State of Bihar (Defendant No. 1) and Dalmia Jain & Co. Ltd. (Defendant No. 2). The case history involves complex interactions between prior leases, alleged contract formation, procedural objections regarding title and statutory compliance, and competing equitable remedies.

**Prior Lease and Contract Formation**
The factual matrix begins with Defendant No. 1 owning the Murli Hills. On April 1, 1928, Defendant No. 1 leased the hills to Kuchwar Lime and Stone Co. (Kuchwar Co.) for 20 years. This lease contained an express prohibition against assignment without Government permission [S830e8b76ae83]. In January 1933, Kuchwar Co. went into liquidation, and its liquidators purported to assign the leasehold interest to Subodh Gopal Bose for Rs. 35,000 via an unregistered deed dated September 30, 1933 [S49406c28d920]. The Government considered this a breach, stopped working orders on December 8, 1933, and subsequently forfeited the lease in favor of Kuchwar Co. by order dated March 27, 1934, re-entering possession [Sa7d4a6c96918].

Following the forfeiture, the Lime Co. applied for a new lease on January 25, 1934 [Sa9e8aaafd99d]. The Board of Revenue approved the execution of the lease but conditioned the issuance of the letter on receiving the Government order cancelling the old lease [Sa7d4a6c96918]. On May 1, 1934, Defendant No. 1 offered to grant leases to the Lime Co. for 20 years on existing terms per Chapter V of the Bihar & Orissa Waste Lands & Mineral Concession Manual [S2c4036b2445a]. The Lime Co. accepted this offer on April 15, 1934, and obtained possession on that date, though the leases were to take effect from April 1, 1934 [S2c4036b2445a]. The trial court found that these exchanges constituted a valid agreement for lease [S06cd204b2cf0].

**Competing Paths: Specific Performance vs. Compensation**
The core legal conflict arises from the validity of the Lime Co.'s title vis-à-vis the Kuchwar Co.'s rights. While the Lime Co. was in possession, Kuchwar Co. sued the Secretary of State for India. Although dismissed at trial, the High Court of Patna decreed the suit on February 7, 1936, declaring the forfeiture invalid [Sd6c529f926cc]. This decision was affirmed by the Privy Council on November 19, 1937 [Sc0a06713e0fd]. Consequently, Kuchwar Co. was reinstated into possession. The Lime Co., not being a party to the Kuchwar suit, continued to remain in possession initially but vacated the quarries in April 1936 after contempt proceedings against its directors [S6e36386cb99b]. Although the Privy Council later set aside the contempt order on October 31, 1938, the Lime Co. did not succeed in getting restitution [S6e36386cb99b].

The Lime Co. argued that both it and Defendant No. 1 proceeded on the assumption that Defendant No. 1 was competent to lease the property [S75fed3609fe9]. When Kuchwar Co.'s original lease expired on March 31, 1948, Defendant No. 1 re-entered possession. The Lime Co. repeatedly asked Defendant No. 1 to execute the agreed leases, but Defendant No. 1 refused and instead decided to lease the Murli Hill to Defendant No. 2 on June 2, 1949 [S106d60d4a58a]. The Lime Co. then sought specific performance and compensation.

**Procedural Objections and Legal Conditions**
Defendant No. 1 resisted the suit on grounds including no concluded contract, limitation, estoppel, acquiescence, and waiver [S9d91cc92c6cb]. Defendant No. 2 denied the Lime Co.'s legal existence and right to sue, arguing that the Government's sanction was based on misapprehension of facts and had no binding effect [Sbb7de2829ba0]. Defendant No. 2 also claimed protection as a subsequent lessee for valuable consideration [S575f63eec68a].

The trial court framed issues regarding the existence of a valid contract and whether the agreement was defective for lack of essential terms or uncertainty [Sea59ce9cf59a, S80dc026f442c]. The trial court held in favor of the Lime Co., finding a valid contract existed [S06cd204b2cf0] and rejecting pleas of limitation and estoppel [Sbeb571c7196c]. It decreed specific performance and compensation from April 1, 1948 [S97682527e61d].

However, the High Court reversed this decree. The High Court judges concurred that a contract was made out but held that the specific contract pleaded was not the one entered into. Crucially, they declared the agreement void under Section 20 of the Indian Contract Act due to mutual mistake of fact regarding the Government's title to the subject matter [S4da221281e65]. They further held it void under Section 30 of the Government of India Act, 1915, because conditions laid down in that section were not complied with [S4da221281e65]. The High Court noted that relief under Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act could not be granted as it would amount to reconstructing the agreement, and alternative relief under Section 15 was unavailable because the Lime Co. had not relinquished all further claims [S4da221281e65, S952f65c826eb]. The High Court also found the Lime Co. was not ready and willing to perform its part of the contract and was not the real plaintiff [S06087d490791].

**Waiver and Estoppel Considerations**
The record highlights tensions regarding waiver and estoppel. Under the Transfer of Property Act, Section 112, waiver of forfeiture requires acceptance of rent or other acts showing intention to treat the lease as subsisting, provided the lessor is aware of the forfeiture [L625a28da96a6]. The Lime Co. relied on the conduct of Defendant No. 1 in offering and accepting applications for new leases after the purported forfeiture of the Kuchwar lease. However, the High Court's finding of mutual mistake regarding title undermines the application of estoppel principles that might otherwise bind the Government to its representations if the underlying transaction was void ab initio due to lack of authority or title [L65ec615070d2].

Furthermore, the issue of res judicata [L193e14a39240] is relevant given the prior litigation between Kuchwar Co. and the Secretary of State. The Lime Co. was not impleaded in that suit [Sc0a06713e0fd], which allowed it to continue in possession temporarily, but the final determination of title in favor of Kuchwar Co. effectively destroyed the premise of the Lime Co.'s claim to specific performance of a lease from a landlord who lacked the immediate right to grant such a lease during the period of Kuchwar's restored title.

**Remaining Gaps and Conclusion**
The available record shows a decisive shift from the trial court's enforcement of the contract to the High Court's dismissal based on substantive defects in title and statutory non-compliance. The Lime Co.'s path to specific performance was blocked by the finding that the contract was void due to mutual mistake of fact (title) and failure to comply with Section 30 of the Government of India Act, 1915 [S4da221281e65]. The attempt to seek compensation or alternative relief failed because the Lime Co. did not strictly adhere to the requirements of Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act, specifically the relinquishment of all claims for deficiency or damages for prior periods [S952f65c826eb, S7093796118f1]. The procedural objection that the Lime Co. was not the 'real plaintiff' and lacked readiness/willingness further complicated its position [S06087d490791]. Thus, the competing paths collapsed: specific performance was barred by the void nature of the agreement regarding title, and compensation/equitable relief was barred by procedural failures in pleading and relinquishing claims.
